entries.title: Everything You Need to Know for Commanders vs. Cowboys
entries.summary: Can Terry McLaurin get back on track as Washington seeks to avoid starting out 0-2?
entries.content:
The Commanders are looking to rebound from a tough season-opening loss to the Eagles and avoid going into an 0-2 hole ahead of a Week 3 meeting against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks. They’ll be facing a Cowboys team that’s similarly in need of a victory.

Here’s everything you need to know.

Kickoff: 4:25 p.m. at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas

TV: Fox

Betting Lines:
Lines from DraftKings, as of Friday. 

Spread: Commanders +4.5
Money line: Commanders +180, Cowboys -218
Over/under: 50.5 points

Pregame Reading

The Commanders new stadium won’t open for four years but new renderings released on Wednesday show the team is looking to address issues that currently hinder its current stadium.

The Commanders lost a nail biter in their season opener and had costly mistakes on both sides of the ball. The Washington Sun's Martenzie Johnson compiled all of the plays that factored into the loss.

Stefon Diggs’ first touchdown for his hometown team had a costly impact on his team’s ability to tie the game early in the fourth quarter. He expressed remorse over his unnecessary penalty.

The season-opening loss to the Eagles laid bare one of the biggest questions facing Washington and its first-time offensive coordinator this season: Should the Commanders protect Jayden Daniels with a more conservative system or let him loose in hopes of recapturing the magic of 2024? The Sun's Dave Sheinin broke down how the team tried to do a little of both against Philadelphia, with mixed results.

About the Cowboys

A trendy preseason pick to make the NFC playoffs, the Cowboys had a disappointing start to their 2026 campaign, losing to the Giants 28-20 on “Sunday Night Football.” Most notably, Dallas’ offense was much less explosive than expected, with star receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens held to a meager 44 and 28 receiving yards, respectively, and running back Javonte Williams rushing for just 41.

Read more about Pickens’ rough season opener in The Dallas Morning News, and about the team’s Week 1 defensive lapses in The Athletic.

One Big Question

Can Terry McLaurin get on track?

First-year offensive coordinator David Blough has discussed getting McLaurin roughly 10 targets per game, but the 31-year-old receiver was a non-factor in the season opener. He caught just two passes for 14 yards on four targets.

McLaurin was limited to just 10 games in 2025 and his 582 receiving yards were the lowest of his career. The Commanders’ offense already has limitations, and can’t afford to have McLaurin held in check for the second straight week.

Quote of the Week

“That wasn’t a coaching thing,” Commanders cornerback Mike Sainristil told reporters Monday. “That wasn’t a schematic thing. That was just two plays on my end with a … I guess you could call it a lack of effort.”

Sainristil ranked last among the 89 cornerbacks Pro Football Focus graded in Week 1, and admitted that two big plays he allowed in Philadelphia stemmed from his effort. Quinn referred to Sainristill’s performance as “completely not acceptable.” He and the team’s secondary could have their hands full covering Lamb and Pickens on Sunday.

entries.title: MS NOW, CNN Say the White House Turned Away Their Journalists
entries.summary: The badges were reportedly revoked a day after Trump announced he was banning the outlet from the building.
entries.content:
MS NOW and CNN said White House officials denied access to at least three of their journalists on Saturday morning, a day after President Donald Trump announced he was banning the two outlets and Politico from the White House.

MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said while she was able to enter two gates within the grounds with no issues, her badge did not scan once inside the building.

“The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said it was disabled, I asked why I was not able to get inside — he said it was ‘above him,’” Gardner said on air, adding that the guard had revoked access from an MS NOW photographer as well.

Another network producer’s badge scanned successfully and she was allowed access on Saturday morning, Gardner said.

“The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS NOW said in a statement. “MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

CNN journalist Betsy Klein was also denied access to the White House grounds Saturday morning, the outlet reported.

Trump posted on Truth Social on Friday that he was banning MS NOW, Politico and CNN journalists because of the outlets’ “constant” fake reports. His announcement did not include additional details.

When reporters later asked how the ban would work in practice, the president said it would be “a very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here.”

Trump also suggested he could ban other outlets, including The New York Times and The Washington Post.

When asked for additional details on Saturday, the White House referred The Washington Sun to Trump’s earlier comments in the Oval Office.
entries.author: Marissa Martinez

entries.title: Cade Cavalli Got His Big Contract. Then He Showed Everyone Why.
entries.summary: The Nationals won big Friday night, after reaching a contract extension with their ace.
entries.content:
ST. LOUIS — Everyone wanted to talk to Cade Cavalli on Friday afternoon, which is what happens when a player signs a four-year, many-million-dollar contract extension. And yet no one could talk to Cavalli in the visitors clubhouse at Busch Stadium, which was because of one of baseball’s unwritten rules: Leave the starting pitching alone. Act like he doesn’t exist. If you happen to lock eyes with him, look away, even when — or, really, especially when — he just made life-changing money to keep pitching for the team that drafted him.

So the most important person in the room was also the loneliest.

Cavalli, white binder in his lap, flipped through a scouting report of the Cardinals, the club he would face (and shut down) in a 9-1 win for the Nationals on Friday night. He nodded along to the music playing through his earbuds. He wore a red beanie, as he always does before starts, no matter the 98-degree heat outside.

Routines are sacred like that in professional sports, where control is the myth that keeps on giving. Which was also why, as the game crept closer, as his teammates laced their cleats, stretched and talked to one another, Cavalli spun his chair around and stared into his locker. He likes to visualize things before they happen, at least as best he can. He’s been doing this a long time, too, ever since grade school, when he picked up a pencil and wrote on notebook paper: When I grow up I want to be a baseball player. 

Getting there is a giant achievement. Building a career, though, sticking around, that’s a whole other challenge, which Cavalli is now well into solving. About an hour earlier Friday afternoon, the Nats had announced his extension, four years plus a club option for 2031. While he studied the Cardinals’ hitters in the clubhouse, the rest of the details were trickling out on social media. The deal will pay Cavalli $47 million across the next four seasons, according to two people familiar with the terms. If the Nationals exercise their option on the back end, the total value could reach $70 million. That means Cavalli could lead the Nats’ rotation for the next half decade.

“You all have seen it: He’s been one of the most consistent pitchers over the course of the last couple months,” Paul Toboni, the Nationals’ president of baseball operations, said Friday. “I thought he really turned the corner. Early in the year, he was a good pitcher. And I think lately he’s become great — and great in a way that has been extremely consistent.”

A first-round pick in 2020, Cavalli has a 3.02 ERA in 167 ⅔ innings. That included 13 strikeouts against the Red Sox on June 3, a career night clouded by Cavalli shouting “Sit down boy!” after striking out a Latin American player, for which he apologized the next day. His season has also included an eight-inning, no-runs, 10-strikeout gem against the Cubs on Aug. 13, then 11 strikeouts in his next outing. These were the flashes of a shut-down ace, all after Cavalli missed almost three full years with arm injuries.

But his most recent innings — the five he threw in St. Louis on Friday — hit in a different way. There’s just something about a good first impression after a team invests in you. Cavalli struck out the side in the first, his fastball popping at 96 mph. In the second, two batters reached with singles, though neither scored. The Nats, meanwhile, put up three in the first and four more in the third. The temperature settled at a sticky 87. And Cavalli never let the Cardinals think about biting into a massive deficit.

He allowed four hits, walked none and got the Cardinals to whiff on five of the 12 curveballs they swung at. When he struck out JJ Wetherholt to end the fifth, he reached 200 strikeouts for the season, the first Nats pitcher to do that since Max Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin all did in 2019. That was also it for Cavalli’s night.

Then, afterward, he could finally talk about the ways his life had suddenly changed.

“I knew that I wanted to be in D.C. as long as possible,” Cavalli said. “I’ve had talks with somebody that I really look up to and envy, Ryan Zimmerman. To see him be part of the organization, the loyalty that came with him. He went through some rough years and then you look up and he’s a World Series winner.”

There are other angles to this, about money and roster-building and whether it means the Nationals will keep more young talent in D.C. They have often struggled with that last part, which you intimately know if you own a Juan Soto, Trea Turner or Anthony Rendon jersey. And an extension for Cavalli doesn’t automatically mean the team will find the right years and dollars for, say, Daylen Lile, let alone James Wood or CJ Abrams.

Plus, in the bigger picture, Cavalli’s extension isn’t necessarily breaking the bank. It buys out his last three years of arbitration eligibility and what could have been his first season on the open market. Beyond that, his performance (and health) between 2027 and 2030 will dictate whether a $23 million option is advantageous for the Nationals, who will have a lot of data before making that choice. But if nothing else, the deal signals a willingness — by ownership and the new front office — to shoulder some level of financial risk to start building a real core.

Toboni and manager Blake Butera hope other players notice.

“We want homegrown players to know that if they come here and carry themselves the right way, go about their work the right way, go out and perform, be great teammates and great leaders, there’s a pathway to be here for the long-term,” Toboni said. “Especially when there’s interest on both sides.”
entries.author: Jesse Dougherty

entries.title: Activists Rally to Reopen Kennedy Center As Its Future Remains Uncertain
entries.summary: An estimated 1,000 people showed up Friday evening in support of keeping the building open as demolition fears grow.
entries.content:
Laura Bligh worked at the Kennedy Center three decades ago. Now retired, she has returned to the institution several times a week to protest President Donald Trump’s reshaping of the storied arts center.

Most days, Bligh has been the only protester outside the building. But Friday night, the crowd was a thousand times bigger.

“I am delighted because it helps show that the people in the D.C. area really love and care about the Kennedy Center. It’s very precious to us,” Bligh told The Washington Sun on Friday.

The demonstration came at a pivotal moment for the Kennedy Center, which closed Tuesday after its Trump-aligned board voted to shutter the venue for repairs — after which a federal judge ordered the administration to provide 30 days’ notice before any major renovations or demolition. Trump continued to bash the building as decrepit this week — and was photographed viewing potential demolition plans on Air Force One — while insisting his name needs to be permanently etched into the facade.

“I'm ready to fix it, make it good,” Trump told reporters at the Oval Office on Friday afternoon. “The Kennedy Center, for 25 years, has lost a tremendous amount of money, and all I'm saying is, I don't mind doing the job, but if I do the job, I think the Trump administration … the Trump administration should be recognized.”

“I'll do a better job building it than anybody else, anybody in America,” Trump added.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Friday evening’s protest, organized by Hands Off the Arts, had been planned for weeks but took on added significance after the closure. Organizers said they formed the group last year in response to firings and layoffs at the Kennedy Center.

The center saw another wave of layoffs that impacted more than a dozen employees on Friday, The Washington Post reported that evening, including top spokesperson Roma Daravi and board relations head Joe LaFauci.

Many attendees brought signs. Some dressed up in inflatable costumes, others brought instruments. Together, they advocated for reopening the Kennedy Center and reinstalling a bipartisan board of trustees that doesn’t include Trump as a chairman.

“Hands off the arts!” the crowd chanted as protesters wrapped around the front and sides of the building, eventually forming a human chain.
_MG_0767 copy.jpg (5599x3733, AR: 1.50)The demonstration drew several elected officials and public figures, including Robert White, the Democratic nominee for D.C.’s congressional delegate; Reps. Don Beyer (D-Virginia) and Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois); Metropolitan Washington Council President Sam Epps and “Wonder Woman” actress Lynda Carter.

Mallory Miller, a co-founder of Hands Off the Arts who was fired from the Kennedy Center last August, said the institution represents an important part of American cultural life. Her comments echoed the broader concerns of protesters who oppose Trump’s involvement in the center.

“The Kennedy Center, to me, is our country’s highest form of self-expression,” Miller told The Sun. “It’s really meaningful, not just for Washingtonians, but for Americans. The fact that it's closed right now is an abomination to our democracy.”

Trump began denouncing the institution’s programming in February 2025, saying the center didn’t need to be “woke” and criticizing some of its performances. He also said the center would no longer host “drag shows, or other anti-American propaganda.”

Tara Hoot, a drag performer who has participated in many Kennedy Center protests, said the size of Friday’s crowd showed growing attention to the dispute.

“It's a presidential memorial and that, first and foremost, should send shock waves around America that the president is trying to slap his name above that of an assassinated president,” Hoot said.
_MG_1110 copy.jpg (5695x3796, AR: 1.50)
Local musicians and performers also took part, including the Gay Men’s Chorus of Washington and the Rapid Response Choir. The evening ended with the crowd singing “America the Beautiful” outside the front of the institution.

Chris Raleigh, another Hands Off the Arts co-founder, told The Sun that the goal of the protest was to prevent Trump from “turning arts and culture on us for his authoritarian project.”

Raleigh gave Trump an ultimatum while speaking to a cheering crowd.

“We will come here again and again, with greater numbers, to embarrass you and show the world how badly you messed up,” Raleigh said.

“Or, Mr. President, you take my deal — bring back the bipartisan board that used to run this place. Bring back the professionals, everyone who used to work in this building,” he said. “Don't lay a finger on JFK's memorial. Open up the building and put art on the damn stages.”
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: Trump Pledges to Appoint an ‘AI Czar’ as He Defends the Technology
entries.summary: The president did not detail what the office’s responsibilities would look like or who he could appoint to the role.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he will soon appoint an artificial intelligence czar amid heightened scrutiny of whether the technology is progressing at a dangerous pace, he announced Saturday on Truth Social.

In a long post defending the industry, Trump said he would create an “AI Force” without specifying its exact functions. He added that in his capacity as president, he would “not stand by” and allow its “decimation, or destruction.”

Lawmakers and tech leaders have sounded the alarm in recent weeks over the advancement of AI and its potential threat to society — including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called for AI companies like his own to slow the technology’s progression last week. Trump has repeatedly pushed back against such concerns and framed AI development as an innovation race between the United States and China.

The president wrote on Truth Social that he believed AI is the “next Industrial Revolution” that could potentially make up “as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP.”

“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump wrote. “Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!”

Trump didn’t provide further detail about what the AI czar’s responsibilities would be or who he was considering for the role, only that he planned to announce the appointment soon.

In a separate post on Truth Social, Trump floated alternatives for a “far more elegant and accurate description” of the technology, suggesting a rebrand of “Superior Intelligence,” “Extreme Intelligence” or “Supreme Intelligence.”

AI is expected to be a point of contentious discussion when Chinese President Xi Jinping visits the White House next week for the first time in more than a decade. The Trump administration has also reportedly invited several technology executives to the state dinner, among them AI developers Jensen Huang of Nvidia and OpenAI’s Sam Altman.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
